Formar o dativo no singular e no plural: Form the dative in the singular and plural and use it for «for whom», age, sensations and verbs like звонить, помогать and нравиться.
(ou: o caso das coisas que acontecem con: (or: the case of the things that happen to us)
Uma cena que você já viveu (ou vai viver: Picture a scene you will probably live. You are in Russia and you are cold. You want to say "I am cold". You think: "cold in Russian is хо́лодно, so I will say я хо́лодно." The person gives you a puzzled look and corrects you: — Мне хо́лодно. You stare. A new word, мне, that you have never seen. You wonder: "Why can't I just say я хо́лодно?" And the person explains: — Because the cold is not yours. The cold happens to you. That is the doorway into the dative case, and it shows one of the most beautiful ideas in Russian. Pay attention: after this lesson you will see the language with new eyes.
O que é o caso dativo? (a verdade filosó: What is the dative case? (the idea behind the grammar)

What is the dative case? Before any table, one question. In English grammar, the dative is the case of the "indirect object". It is the case of "to" and "for": "I gave the book to Ivan." "I spoke to Maria." "I bought a present for you." The dative belongs to the one who receives the action, not the one who does it. But that definition is dry. Here is the one that changes everything: the dative is the case of things that happen TO US but are not OURS. Think about it. Heat. Cold. Hunger. Thirst. Pleasure. Displeasure. Liking. Needing. Hurting. All of these happen to us, but we do not do them. They come from outside and reach us. In English we say: I am hot. I am cold. I like coffee. I need help. I feel pain. Notice that every sentence starts with I, as if the heat, the cold, the liking, the need and the pain were things we own. But they are not. The heat is not yours; it happens to you. The cold is not yours; it happens to you. The coffee pleases you. Help is missing for you. Russian captures this precisely, and all of these go into the dative. Look: the "I" disappears and мне comes in. The verb "to be" also disappears (you know that from Lesson 4). The sentence becomes: "To me — hot." "To me — cold." "To me — pleasing is the coffee." It is a mental revolution: Russian does not say that you are hot, it says that it is hot to you. English has a faint echo of this: "it seems to me", "it is all the same to me", "it occurs to me". Russian does it for dozens of everyday ideas.

O dativo: «para mim» e os pronomes: The dative: "to me" and the pronouns
O caso dativo é o caso do \"para mim, a: The dative is the case of "to me, for me". Before the deep idea, let us be practical. In its simplest form the dative is the case of "to" and "for" someone: the receiver. To me — мне. For me — мне. I gave the book to Ivan — я дал кни́гу Ива́ну. I spoke to Maria — я сказа́л Мари́и. I bought a present for you — я купи́л пода́рок тебе́. These are the most obvious uses. If you understood the accusative (the case of the action) and the prepositional (the case of place), the dative is the case of the recipient: the one who receives something. But the dative is much more than that. It is also the case of: physical states (cold, heat, hunger, thirst); emotional states (sad, glad, bad, well); liking (нра́виться); needing (ну́жно, нужна́); age (мне 20 лет); verbs such as help, phone, tell, write (to someone). All of this is dative, because all of it is something that happens to you, not something you do. First step: the personal pronouns in the dative. They are the foundation; without them you will not get far. Here they are. Notice: мне (to me) looks like меня́ (accusative), but with -е instead of -я. тебе́ (to you) looks like тебя́ (accusative), but with -е. ему́ and ей (to him, to her) are forms of their own, and нам / вам / им are short and easy to memorise. How to use them: learn them like magic words. They will appear in almost every sentence you build.

A grande distinção: o que VOCÊ FAZ vs. o: The big distinction: what YOU DO vs. what HAPPENS to you

This is the most important idea of the lesson. Russian has two ways of linking a person and a thing: STEP 1: the person DOES an action. The verb is active, the person is the subject and the thing is the object (accusative). STEP 2: a thing HAPPENS to the person. The verb is impersonal or describes a feeling, and the person is in the dative. Compare. What YOU DO (accusative) versus what HAPPENS to you (dative). Notice: in the first list I am the subject. I do the action: I love, I read, I see. In the second list the thing happens to me: the cold happens to me, the coffee pleases me, the need comes to me, the years are counted to me. Russian separates the two firmly. English speakers always start with "I": "I am cold." "I like coffee." "I am 20." Russian answers: "No. It is not yours. It happens to you. Use the dative."
A mim é frio. (Eu estou com frio.): To me it is cold. (I am cold.)
A mim é quente. (Eu estou com calor.): To me it is hot. (I am hot.)
A mim \\[me\\] apetece comer. (Estou com: To me \[it\] feels like eating. (I am hungry.)
A mim agrada o café. (Eu gosto de café.): To me the coffee is pleasing. (I like coffee.)
A mim é necessário trabalhar. (Eu precis: To me it is necessary to work. (I need to work.)
To me are twenty years. (I am 20 years old.)
A ilusão do \"eu estou com calor\". Vou: Here is a small secret nobody tells you. In English we say "I am hot" or "I have a headache", as if the heat or the pain were something we carry, a temporary possession. But the heat belongs to the room. It happens to you. You do not carry it; it wraps around you and arrives without being asked. Russian understands this. So in Russian you do not say "I am hot". You say: Мне жа́рко. (To me [it is] hot.) The heat is not mine; it happens to me. The "I" is not the subject but the dative. Try the test with other sensations: in Russian they all go into the dative, because they are things that happen to you, not things you own. Notice that the pattern is always мне + a word. The word can be an adverb (хо́лодно, жа́рко, пло́хо, хорошо́) or a verb (хо́чется). But мне is always there. This is one of the most used constructions in Russian. Every day you will say "мне хо́лодно" a thousand times, and "мне жа́рко", and "мне ну́жно". You are not "doing" the cold; you are "having" it, in the dative.
O dativo responde a «кому? чему?» (a que: The dative answers «кому? чему?» (to whom? to what?). In English we use "to" or "for" + someone: "I give the book to my brother." In Russian the word changes its ending. Singular, masculine and neuter: consonant + -у (брат → брату); -й and -ь become -ю (учитель → учителю); -о becomes -у (окно → окну); -е becomes -ю (море → морю). Feminine: -а and -я become -е (мама → маме, неделя → неделе); -ия becomes -ии (Мария → Марии); -ь becomes -и (ночь → ночи). Plural, for all genders: -ам or -ям (студенты → студентам, друзья → друзьям). Irregular: дочь → дочери, мать → матери.

Verbos e preposições com dativo: Verbs and prepositions with the dative
A grande distinção: GOSTAR vs. AMAR: The big distinction: LIKING vs. LOVING
A grande distinção: GOSTAR vs. AMAR. Aqu: This is the most charming part of Russian, and English hides it. In English we use "love" and "like" as the same thing at two strengths: I love Maria (intense). I like coffee (milder). Both are normal active verbs with "I" as the subject. Russian splits them by structure. ЛЮБИТЬ — to love (I do the action). Люби́ть works like "love": the subject is the person, the object is in the accusative. Notice that люби́ть takes the accusative (Мари́ю, кни́гу, жену́, роди́ну). Love is an action that leaves you. You are the agent. НРАВИТЬСЯ — to be pleasing, to like (the thing comes to you). Нра́виться works differently. Russian does not say "I like coffee". It says: Мне нра́вится ко́фе. (To me the coffee is pleasing.) Мне is the dative (to me). нра́вится is the verb (is pleasing). ко́фе is the SUBJECT of the sentence. In Russian the coffee is the one acting; it pleases me. Pleasure travels from the coffee to me, and I am in the dative because it happens to me. English has the same pattern in "the coffee appeals to me" or "that idea pleases me". Two important points: STEP 1: the verb agrees with the thing, not the person. Мне нра́вится ко́фе (singular, because ко́фе is singular). Мне нра́вятся кни́ги (plural, because кни́ги is plural). The person is always мне, ему́, ей, and so on. STEP 2: do not confuse it with люби́ть. The difference in one line: люби́ть, love leaves you, you are the agent, the thing is the object, accusative. Нра́виться, pleasure comes to you, the thing is the agent, you are the receiver, dative. Which to use? If it is a deep, active feeling of yours, люби́ть. If it is something that pleases you, gives you enjoyment, comes from outside, нра́виться. In general: люби́ть is for people (romantic, family love), for one's homeland and for much-loved things. Нра́виться is for food, music, films, cities, things that give pleasure. It also works for people, when the feeling is milder than love. Russian makes you think about where the feeling comes from: love leaves you, pleasure comes to you. Two different things, two verbs, two cases.

Outros usos do dativo: precisar, dever,: Other uses of the dative: need, may, suit, phone

Besides the "philosophical" uses, the dative has very practical ones. Here are the main ones. НУЖНО / НУЖНА́ / НУ́ЖНЫ — to need. In English: "I need something". In Russian: "to me [is] necessary something". The form of ну́жно agrees with the thing needed, not with the person: ну́жно when a verb follows (ну́жно рабо́тать); ну́жен when the noun is masculine; нужна́ when it is feminine; ну́жно when it is neuter; ну́жны when it is plural. The person is always in the dative: Мне ну́жно means "to me [it is] necessary". The need happens to you. НА́ДО — to need (a synonym of ну́жно). На́до works like ну́жно but is more colloquial. МО́ЖНО / НЕЛЬЗЯ́ — may / may not. Мо́жно means "it is possible, it is allowed". Нельзя́ means "it is not possible, it is not allowed". Both take the dative when the person is named. ВОЗМО́ЖНО — possible. Возмо́жно also goes with the dative. The verb НРА́ВИТЬСЯ (seen above): after "to need", it is the most common dative verb. ИДТИ́ — to suit, to look good on. Verbs of communication: помогать, звонить, писать, говорить, давать and so on. All of them put the recipient in the dative. Notice that all these verbs have a recipient, someone who receives the action, and that person goes into the dative. AGE: мне 20 лет. In English: "I am 20". In Russian: "to me [are] 20 years". The logic: age happens to you; you do not own the years. Dative.

Verbos e preposições que pedem dativo: Verbs and prepositions that take the dative
Alguns verbos pedem dativo mesmo quando: Some verbs take the dative even when the English object looks direct: «звонить кому?» (to phone someone), «помогать кому?» (to help someone), «отвечать кому?» (to answer someone), «советовать кому?» (to advise someone). The verb «нравиться» flips the sentence: the person who likes goes into the dative and the thing liked is the subject: «Мне нравится музыка» (the music is pleasing to me). If the thing is plural, the verb is plural too: «Мне нравятся фильмы». The prepositions «к» (towards a person or place: «Я иду к другу») and «по» («по телефону», «по субботам») take the dative.

Substantivos no dativo e tabela mestra: Nouns in the dative and the master table
Nouns in the dative (endings). Now the nouns. How do they change in the dative? The method is the same as always: STEP 1: find the nominative form (the dictionary form). STEP 2: add the dative ending, which depends on the gender and on the ending of the word. STEP 3: done. The dative endings are in the tables below. Notice: masculine (consonant, -й, -ь) takes -У/-Ю. Feminine in -а/-я takes -Е. Feminine in -ь and -ия takes -И/-ИИ. Neuter in -о/-е takes -У/-Ю. Neuter in -мя takes -ЕНИ. The big difference between the dative and the prepositional: masculine and neuter in -о/-е take -У/-Ю, not -Е. Compare. In the masculine and in the neuter in -о, the dative differs from the prepositional. In the feminine, they are the same. Then comes the master table of the dative, which solves everything.

B Tabelas de apoio: Plural, Adjetivos, P: Support tables: plural, adjectives, possessives and the prepositions К and ПО with the dative. Prepositions of the dative: К (КО) = movement towards a person, or a doctor (идти́ к врачу́ = go to the doctor, е́хать к дру́гу = drive to a friend's, ко мне = to my place). ПО = along, by means of, on a subject (гуля́ть по у́лице / по го́роду = walk along the street / around the city, говори́ть по телефо́ну = talk on the phone, кни́га по исто́рии = a book on history). The big difference of the dative: it does two jobs. STEP 1: indirect object (to whom you give, speak, write). STEP 2: logical subject (in impersonal constructions). Notice that it is the same form but a different function. In the first example the dative is the recipient of the action. In the others the dative is the person who experiences a state. That is why the dative matters so much: it appears in two very common types of sentence. Normal sentences with an indirect object: я даю́ ему́ кни́гу. Impersonal sentences: мне хо́лодно, мне нра́вится. Without the dative you can say neither.

Os erros que o brasileiro VAI cometer no: The mistakes English speakers WILL make with the dative. Mistake 1: using the nominative instead of the dative in impersonal constructions. Wrong: Я хо́лодно. Right: Мне хо́лодно. You think "I am cold" and translate word for word into «я хо́лодно». But Russian says «мне хо́лодно»: the I turns into мне (dative). Mistake 2: using the accusative instead of the dative with verbs of communication. Wrong: Я помога́ю его́. Right: Я помога́ю ему́. Помога́ть and other verbs of communication take the dative, not the accusative. In English "help him" looks like a plain object, so this one catches everyone. Verbs that take the dative: помога́ть (help), звони́ть (phone), писа́ть (write to someone), говори́ть (speak to someone), дава́ть (give to someone), расска́зывать (tell someone), улыба́ться (smile at someone), ве́рить (believe someone), меша́ть (disturb someone), зави́довать (envy someone), отвеча́ть (answer someone), дари́ть (give a present to someone), покупа́ть (buy for someone). Mistake 3: using the person as the subject of нра́виться. Wrong: Я нра́влюсь ко́фе. Right: Мне нра́вится ко́фе. Нра́виться is a special verb. It does not go with я; it goes with мне (dative). The subject is the thing, not the person. Ко́фе is the subject, мне is the one it pleases. Mistake 4: mixing up нра́виться and люби́ть. Wrong: Я нра́влю ко́фе. Right: Мне нра́вится ко́фе. (I like coffee.) Люби́ть = to love (an active feeling). Нра́виться = to be pleasing (pleasure that comes from outside). Different verbs with different structures. Mistake 5: using the nominative instead of the dative with ну́жно. Wrong: Я ну́жно рабо́тать. Right: Мне ну́жно рабо́тать. Ну́жно works like «мне хо́лодно»: the person goes into the dative, and the thing that is needed goes into the nominative. Mistake 6: using the wrong noun ending. Wrong: Я помога́ю Мари́я. Right: Я помога́ю Мари́и. Feminine in -ия takes -ии in the dative: Мари́я → Мари́и. Wrong: Я помога́ю друг. Right: Я помога́ю дру́гу. A masculine in a consonant takes -у in the dative. Mistake 7: forgetting that with нра́виться the verb agrees with the thing, not the person. Wrong: Мне нра́вится кни́ги. Right: Мне нра́вятся кни́ги. Кни́ги is plural, so the verb is plural: нра́вятся. Wrong: Мне нра́вятся ко́фе. Right: Мне нра́вится ко́фе. Ко́фе is singular, so the verb stays singular: нра́вится. Mistake 8: building the feeling with a preposition, as English does with "with" or "have". English says "I have a cold" or "I feel the cold". In Russian there is no preposition and no verb "have": just dative + word, мне хо́лодно. Mistake 9: putting «thank you» into the dative. In Russian "thank you" is simply спаси́бо, with no dative. (There is a formal construction благодарю́ вас / благодарю́ тебя́, where the verb благодари́ть takes the accusative.) Mistake 10: forgetting that нужно agrees with the thing needed. Wrong: Мне ну́жно по́мощь. Right: Мне нужна́ по́мощь. По́мощь is feminine, so нужна́, not ну́жно.

Idade, sensações e necessidade com o dat: Age, feelings and need with the dative
Em russo, idade, sensação e necessidade: In Russian, age, feelings and need are said with the dative of the person, with no verb like «to have» or «to be»: «Мне 20 лет» (I am 20); «Мне холодно» (I am cold); «Мне нужно работать» (I need to work).
